64.title: The north wind and the sun
64.hook: the wind's force can't take the traveler's cloak, and the sun's warmth does (Aesop)
64.howItsDone: Aesop's fables are still read with children today, and the north wind and the sun is a common one for talking about persuasion rather than force.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Shekhinah, God's indwelling presence: God lives wherever people let God in. Your line was let it in. Now, a new week: Aesop's fables.

Louder voice. More facts, faster. All caps in the group chat. That's what pushing someone to change their mind looks like, and it tends to backfire: pushed, people fold their arms and hold on harder. So who has ever actually changed your mind, and how did they do it? This week belongs to Aesop. Tradition says he was an enslaved man in ancient Greece who told short stories with animals and weather in them, and a sting at the end.
screen: `CHANGING A MIND BY PUSHING.` → `PEOPLE DIG IN.` → `AESOP, ANCIENT GREECE.`

segments.voice: The north wind and the sun are arguing about which of them is stronger. Then they see a traveler walking along the road, wrapped in a cloak. Whoever gets the cloak off that man, they agree, is the stronger. The north wind goes first. It blows, cold, hard, howling, tearing at the cloak. And the harder it blows, the tighter the traveler pulls the cloak around himself, both hands, head down. The wind blows until it's exhausted, and gives up. Then it's the sun's turn. The sun doesn't push. It just comes out and shines, gently at first, then warmer. The traveler loosens the cloak. Warmer still, and he unwraps it. Finally, too hot to walk another step in it, he takes the cloak off by himself. The sun wins without touching him. The old morals attached to this fable put it in a line: gentle persuasion does what force cannot. A word on Aesop himself: the ancient historian Herodotus mentions him, but the stories we call Aesop's fables were gathered over many centuries, and nobody knows which, if any, he told himself. Now the point. Force creates resistance. Push someone, and they hold on tighter to exactly what you want them to let go of. Warmth makes the letting go their own choice. That doesn't mean never be firm. It means that when you want a person to change, the most powerful thing is often to make it safe for them to take off the cloak.

65.title: The tortoise and the hare
65.hook: the hare naps, and the slow one arrives (Aesop)
65.howItsDone: The tortoise and the hare is often told to children, and "slow and steady wins the race" has become an everyday saying in English.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was gentle persuasion: the sun took the traveler's cloak without touching him. Your line was warmth wins.

This one gets told to children before they can read, which is exactly why it's worth hearing again: the stories learned earliest are the ones people stop listening to. So here's a question to carry through it: in the famous race, why does the tortoise win? The usual answer: because slow and steady wins. But the fable itself is a bit sharper than the saying. A hare is making fun of a tortoise for being so slow. And the tortoise, instead of arguing, says something surprising.
screen: `YOU KNOW THIS ONE.` → `WHY DOES THE TORTOISE WIN?` → `THE HARE MAKES FUN.`

segments.voice: The tortoise says: all right. Let's race. The hare laughs. He's fast, and he knows it. But he agrees, they set a course, and off they go. The hare shoots ahead, and in no time the tortoise is a dot far behind him. So the hare thinks: what's the rush? I could win this in my sleep. He lies down under a tree by the road to rest a little, and falls fast asleep. The tortoise keeps walking. Not fast. Not dramatically. Step, step, step. Past the tree where the hare is snoring, on down the road. When the hare finally wakes up and races to the finish, the tortoise is already there. So why does the tortoise win? Not because slow is better than fast. The hare is faster, and the fable never pretends otherwise. The tortoise wins because he doesn't stop, and the hare does. The hare's real problem isn't his speed; he's so sure of himself he quits in the middle. In a few words: steady effort beats talent that takes a nap. That's good news for anyone who isn't naturally fast at something. You don't have to be brilliant at a thing to get somewhere with it. You have to keep showing up. And here you are, on day sixty-five of this path. Some days were big, some small. Maybe some days you rested, and that's part of it too. But you kept walking, step, step, step. That's how a tortoise gets anywhere.

66.title: The lion and the mouse
66.hook: a spared mouse later gnaws the lion free from a net (Aesop)
66.howItsDone: The lion and the mouse is still told to children as a lesson that even the small can help the strong.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was steady effort: the hare napped, and the tortoise kept walking. Your line was slow and steady.

A flat tire on the highway. A night in the hospital. A week when everything falls apart. The help that shows up in a pinch is often not who anyone would have guessed. Not the important friend, not the boss, not the one with the big job. The neighbor you barely knew. The quiet coworker. The stranger. Aesop has a fable about exactly that, and it starts with a lion asleep in the sun. A little mouse, running about, doesn't look where it's going, and runs right across the lion's face. The lion wakes up, and his huge paw comes down.
screen: `WHO HELPED IN A PINCH?` → `NOT WHO YOU'D HAVE GUESSED.` → `A MOUSE ON A LION'S FACE.`

segments.voice: The mouse is pinned, about to be eaten. And it begs: please, let me go. Spare me, and one day I'll repay you. The lion finds this hilarious. A mouse, repay a lion? But he's amused, and not very hungry, so he lifts his paw, and the mouse runs off. Some time later, the lion is hunting in the forest and walks straight into a trap: a hunters' net. The ropes close around him, and the more he struggles, the tighter it holds. He roars, and the whole forest hears it. So does the mouse. It runs to the net, looks it over, and starts to gnaw. One rope. Then another. Its teeth are tiny, but they're sharp, and it doesn't stop until there's a hole big enough, and the lion walks out free. And the mouse says, more or less: you laughed at me when I said I'd repay you. Now you know even a mouse can help a lion. Two things are going on. First, the obvious one: don't judge who can help you by their size. Small friends matter. Second, look at the lion's kindness. He didn't spare the mouse as an investment. He laughed at the very idea of being repaid. He let it go for nothing, and that's exactly the kind of kindness that comes back in ways nobody could plan. You can't know which small, unrepayable kindness will turn out to be a rope someone gnaws through for you one day. So here's one way to carry it: be kind to the small ones anyway.

67.title: The fox and the grapes
67.hook: what we can't reach, we decide was sour anyway (Aesop)
67.howItsDone: The fox and the grapes is one of Aesop's shortest and best-known fables; the English phrase "sour grapes" comes from it, and psychologists often use it to describe how people cope with disappointment.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was unrepayable kindness: a lion spared a mouse for nothing, and the mouse gnawed him free. Your line was small friends.

You didn't get into the program. A week later you're telling people you never really wanted it: the commute would have been awful, the people seemed stuck-up. Or the relationship ended, and suddenly you can list everything that was wrong from the start. Nearly everyone does this. There's even a two-word English phrase for it, and it comes from a fable traditionally said to be about twenty-five centuries old. A fox is walking along, hungry, on a hot day, and he looks up and sees a bunch of grapes hanging from a vine, dark and ripe and heavy.
screen: `I NEVER REALLY WANTED IT.` → `A TWO-WORD PHRASE.` → `A HUNGRY FOX, HIGH GRAPES.`

segments.voice: The grapes are high, trained up over a branch. The fox backs up, takes a run, and jumps. Misses. Jumps again. His teeth snap on air. He tries again and again, until he's panting and embarrassed. Finally he gives up. He turns, puts his nose in the air, and walks off, saying: I didn't want them anyway. They're sour. In the old Greek versions, he says they're unripe: still green, not worth having. That little line gave English its phrase: sour grapes. Here's what's sharp about it. The fox never tastes the grapes. He learns something about the vine, that it's high, and then he rewrites the grapes so he doesn't have to feel the disappointment. Psychologists have studied this for decades. When there's a gap between what someone wanted and what they got, the gap is uncomfortable, and one common way to close it is to change the story about what they wanted. It works, for a while. It spares the pain. But it costs something. Call every out-of-reach thing sour, and you stop knowing what you actually want. You never ask the useful question: were the grapes too high today, or could I find a ladder? That's today's line: not sour, just high. It's an honest sentence. It lets you admit you wanted it, and that you couldn't reach it, both at once. Sometimes the answer is to let the grapes go. Sometimes it's to come back taller. But you can only choose if you tell the truth about the grapes.

segments.voice: Think of something you once reached for and didn't get, a job, a friendship, a skill, a place, and listen for a little sour-grapes voice in the story you tell about it now. Gently, just to yourself, say the true version: I wanted it, and it was out of reach. Then ask: too high forever, or just too high then?

68.title: The oak and the reeds
68.hook: the oak breaks in the storm, and the reeds bend and live (Aesop)
68.howItsDone: People who read Aesop as everyday wisdom often reach for the oak and the reeds when they talk about flexibility: letting small things pass while keeping one's roots.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was omphax, the unripe grape a fox called sour once he couldn't reach it. Your line was not sour, just high.

A storm is coming over a river valley. The sky goes green, the wind gets loud, and everything standing up has to decide what to do about it. On the bank there's a huge oak, the kind of tree people have picnics under, the kind that looks like it will outlast everyone. And down at the water's edge there's a patch of reeds, thin as pencils, the kind nobody notices. The smart money is on the oak. The people who told this story counted on that.
screen: `A STORM OVER THE RIVER.` → `THE GREAT OAK.` → `THE THIN REEDS.`

segments.voice: It's another of Aesop's fables, and it comes down in more than one version, with one reed or many. Here's one telling. A great wind tears through the valley. The oak stands firm, because that's what oaks do. The wind keeps pushing, and the oak keeps refusing, until with a crack its roots rip out of the bank and it falls into the river. The current carries it downstream, past the reeds, a little ruffled, and fine. The oak asks how they survived, when something so small should have been flattened. And the reeds answer, more or less: you fought the wind, and it broke you. We bowed our heads, and let it pass over us. Look at what that answer isn't. The reeds didn't stop being reeds. When the storm moved on, they stood straight again, rooted in the same mud. Bending isn't the same as being blown away. And the oak's strength was real, and admirable, and no use in this one storm, because it had only one move. Some old versions add a moral: those who yield to what they can't fight come through it. Another reading is quieter. A few things in life are worth standing against. Most of what blows through an ordinary day isn't. A plan changed at the last minute is wind. The way someone loads the dishwasher is wind. Bend, and come back up.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small thing you've been holding stiff about, a plan someone changed, a habit of someone you live with, a word that bugs you, and notice where you hold it in your body, maybe the jaw, maybe the shoulders. Picture the reeds at the water's edge, bowing as the wind goes over, and on each out-breath, let that place bend a little. You're not giving up who you are; you're letting one gust pass.

69.title: The dog and its reflection
69.hook: a dog drops its bone to grab the bigger one in the water (Aesop)
69.howItsDone: Readers of Aesop have long used the dog and its reflection to talk about greed and envy; people who keep a gratitude habit do something similar each day, naming what they already have.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was reeds: the oak fought the wind and fell, and the reeds bowed and stood up again. Your line was bend, don't break.

It finally arrives, the thing you wanted: the phone, the apartment, the job. For about a week, it's wonderful. Then you see someone else's version. A bigger one. A newer one. A better view. And the thing in your hands, the one you were so glad about last Tuesday, suddenly feels small. Nothing about it changed. Only where you were looking. The Greeks had a story for this, and it stars a hungry dog trotting home across a narrow bridge, with dinner in its mouth.
screen: `FINALLY, THE THING YOU WANTED.` → `THEN, A BIGGER ONE.` → `A DOG ON A BRIDGE.`

segments.voice: In the picture books it's a bone. In the old Greek collections of Aesop, it's usually a piece of meat, a real prize for a dog. He's carrying it home across a plank over a stream, or wading a river, depending on the version. He glances down. There in the water is another dog, with another piece of meat, and this one looks bigger. So he does what hungry creatures do. He opens his mouth to snap at the other dog's dinner, and his own piece drops, splashes, and is gone, carried off by the current. And the other dog? Gone too, because it was never there. The water had only shown him himself. He walks home with nothing. The old versions end with a moral about greed: grab for more, and lose what you had. That's true, and it's plenty. But there's a second thing in the story that's easy to miss. The bigger dinner wasn't someone else's at all. It was his own, seen in a different light, looking larger than it was. A lot of what people reach for works like that. Somebody's vacation photos. Somebody's kitchen. Often it's your own ordinary life, reflected back with better lighting. The dog didn't need a bigger piece of meat. He needed to notice the one already in his mouth. That sounds small, and isn't. The Tao Te Ching says something close: whoever knows they have enough is rich. Aesop just says it with a wet, hungry, disappointed dog.

70.title: The ant and the grasshopper
70.hook: the ant stores for winter and turns the singer away, an ending people have argued over for centuries (Aesop)
70.howItsDone: The ant and the grasshopper is often retold: teachers use it for planning ahead, and readers debate whether the ants should have shared.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Aesop, and his dog that dropped its real dinner to snap at a bigger one that was only itself. Your line was hold what you have.

Here's a fable people still argue about. Not over what happens, but over whether the ending is fair. It's the last one of the week with Aesop, after a run of little stories that went a long way. The sun got the cloak off where the wind couldn't. The tortoise arrived. A mouse freed a lion. A fox called the grapes sour. The reeds bent, and the dog lost his dinner to the water. Each one fits in a breath. So does this one.
screen: `THE ONE PEOPLE ARGUE ABOUT.` → `A WEEK OF AESOP.` → `SHORT STORIES, LONG LIVES.`

segments.voice: First, a surprise. In the old Greek versions, it isn't a grasshopper at all. It's a cicada, the insect that sings through the hot months in Greece. All summer the ants work, carrying grain back to their nest, one heavy seed at a time. All summer the cicada sings. Then winter comes. The fields are bare, and the cicada is starving. It comes to the ants and asks them for a little of their food. The ants ask: what were you doing all summer, when you should have been gathering? And the cicada says: I wasn't idle. I was singing. The ants answer, more or less: if you piped all summer, then dance all winter. And they send it away. For a very long time, people read that as the point. Plan ahead. Work while you can. Winter always comes. And that is real wisdom: the ants aren't wrong about winter. But some readers wince at the ending. The ants had enough to spare, and a neighbor was hungry at the door. Is that wisdom, or is it just being right? Some later retellings change the ending: the ants take the singer in, and its music gets them through the long dark months. This path doesn't have to pick one ending. Today's line holds both halves. Store, like the ant: put something by, because winter is real. And share, because a full storehouse and a hungry neighbor at the door is its own kind of story. The old fable shuts the door. What happens at yours is the open question.

segments.voice: Think of one small thing you could put by for later, a few dollars, an hour of sleep, the leftovers, a bit of energy you don't have to spend, and picture setting it aside, like an ant with one seed. Then think of one small thing you could give, a snack, a message, some time, a song, and picture handing it over. Hold both pictures, one in each hand.
cicada. In the old Greek original, it sang all summer while the ants stored grain, and was turned away in winter.
Your line: store, and share. Winter is real, and so is the neighbor at the door. That's seventy days, and a week of Aesop.

myth: in the old Greek versions, the singer is a grasshopper
it's a cicada, the insect that sings through the Greek summer.
readers have argued about whether the ending is fair
they still do. some later retellings have the ants share.
the ants in the old version share their grain
they tell the singer to dance all winter, and send it away.

fork.setup: you're the ants. it's winter, your nest is full, and the hungry singer is at the door. what does the old fable have you do?
options: share half your grain
send it away: dance all winter, then
take it in and ask for songs
fork.reveal: in the old versions the ants send it away. later retellings sometimes change the ending, and readers still argue about it.

original.note: Greek: cicada. the singer in the old Greek fable, later turned into a grasshopper.

trapdoor: what you thought: work hard, and don't be a grasshopper.
what it means: winter is real, so store; a neighbor at the door is real too, so share.
what a scholar hears: in the Greek it's a cicada (tettix); later retellers, like La Fontaine, kept the sharp ending.

sources.ref: Fables I.1, La Cigale et la Fourmi
